# World Streaming and Data Residency

> **Draft chapter map.** Explain how a large world becomes available gradually under explicit memory, bandwidth, and latency budgets.

## A World Is Not All Resident

- Distinguish the logical world from the subset currently loaded into CPU and GPU memory.
- Explain why streaming is an engine-wide coordination problem rather than a file-loading feature.

### Spatial Partitioning and Entity Residency

- Introduce cells, regions, and demand sources such as players, cameras, and gameplay triggers.
- Explain the lifecycle of entities entering and leaving residency.

#### Detail Streaming

- Separate existence of a world object from the fidelity of its visual and audio data.
- Connect detail decisions to visibility and quality budgets.

## Demand, Fulfilment, and Arbitration

- Present streaming as requests competing for limited IO, CPU, upload, and memory capacity.
- Explain priorities, cancellation, and starvation avoidance.

### Streaming Across Engine Domains

- Show the contracts among World, assets, renderer, and persistence.
- Emphasize that the game asks for intent while engine services arbitrate realization.

#### Loading Screens and Live Worlds

- Explain why an existing World can remain interactive while a successor loads.
- Connect world transitions to lifecycle and UI contracts.

## Persistence and Change

- Distinguish base world data from player or simulation changes.
- Explain save/load as a data-model problem before choosing a file format.

### Base-and-Overlay Models

- Describe layering authored content with runtime deltas.
- Discuss conflict, versioning, and migration at a conceptual level.

#### Failure and Recovery

- Cover missing cells, partial loads, invalid data, and budget exhaustion.
- Relate graceful degradation to explicit engine policy.
